Adair: Columbia is home to Lindsey Wilson College, and novelist Janice Holt Giles wrote most of her Kentucky books from a farm near Knifley.
Allen: Dollar General traces its roots to Scottsville, where J.L. Turner started the business that became the chain in 1939.
Anderson: Lawrenceburg punches far above its weight in bourbon: both Wild Turkey and Four Roses distill here.
Ballard: Wickliffe Mounds preserves a Mississippian village occupied around 1100–1350 AD, right where the Ohio meets the Mississippi.
Barren: Named for the "barrens," the prairie-like grasslands early settlers found here — which turned out to be some of the most fertile land in the state.
Bath: Named for its mineral springs; Olympian Springs was one of the earliest resort spas west of the Alleghenies.
Bell: Pine Mountain State Resort Park, opened in 1924, was Kentucky's very first state park.
Boone: Big Bone Lick is called the birthplace of American vertebrate paleontology; Thomas Jefferson had mastodon bones from here shipped east.
Bourbon: Claiborne Farm near Paris was home to Secretariat, who is buried there — given the rare honor of a full-body burial.
Boyd: Ashland produced an unusual density of country music royalty, including Naomi and Wynonna Judd and Billy Ray Cyrus.
Boyle: In 1809 in Danville, Dr. Ephraim McDowell performed the world's first successful ovarian tumor removal — without anesthesia.
Bracken: George Clooney grew up in Augusta, the little river town on the Ohio.
Breathitt: Nicknamed "Bloody Breathitt" for its feuds, it later became known as the county that filled its WWI quota entirely with volunteers.
Breckinridge: Named for John Breckinridge, who drafted the Kentucky Resolutions of 1798 and later served as Jefferson's Attorney General.
Bullitt: Bernheim Arboretum and Research Forest covers more than 16,000 acres, one of the largest privately owned nature preserves in the U.S.
Butler: The Green River, which winds through the county, is one of the most biologically diverse river systems in North America.
Caldwell: Princeton was a flashpoint of the Black Patch War, when tobacco Night Riders burned warehouses in 1906.
Calloway: Murray calls itself the "Birthplace of Radio," for Nathan Stubblefield's wireless voice transmission experiments in the 1890s.
Campbell: Newport was the notorious "Sin City" of the Midwest, packed with illegal casinos until reformers cleaned it up in 1961.
Carlisle: Formed in 1886, it's one of Kentucky's least populous counties and sits at the far western edge along the Mississippi.
Carroll: Carrollton sits at the confluence of the Kentucky and Ohio rivers, a spot Native peoples and early settlers both prized.
Carter: Carter Caves State Resort Park has more than 20 known caves plus several natural bridges, including one you can drive over.
Casey: Liberty's Apple Festival has produced enormous apple pies, baked in a custom-built pan that's become the town's mascot.
Christian: Hopkinsville rebranded itself "Eclipseville" for the 2017 total solar eclipse, sitting at the point of greatest duration.
Clark: Ale-8-One, the ginger-citrus soft drink invented in 1926, is still bottled only in Winchester.
Clay: The salt licks along Goose Creek made this one of the most important salt-producing regions in the early West.
Clinton: The all-tackle world record smallmouth bass — 11 lbs 15 oz — was pulled out of Dale Hollow Lake in 1955 and still stands.
Crittenden: Marion was the heart of America's fluorspar mining district; the Clement Mineral Museum holds a world-class collection.
Cumberland: The nation's first commercial oil well was drilled near Burkesville in 1818 — by accident, while looking for salt brine.
Daviess: Owensboro is home to the Bluegrass Music Hall of Fame and a barbecue tradition built on mutton, which is rare in the U.S.
Edmonson: Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system on Earth, with more than 400 mapped miles and more found every year.
Elliott: It voted Democratic in every single presidential election from its founding in 1869 until 2012 — one of the longest streaks in the country.
Estill: Fitchburg Furnace, built in 1869, is one of the largest stone iron furnaces ever constructed in the United States.
Fayette: Lexington bills itself the Horse Capital of the World; the city and county merged into one government in 1974.
Fleming: Known as the Covered Bridge Capital of Kentucky, with three 19th-century covered bridges still standing.
Floyd: Prestonsburg's Jenny Wiley Theatre keeps alive the story of a frontier woman who escaped captivity and walked home.
Franklin: Frankfort is one of the smallest state capitals in the country; Daniel Boone is buried on the bluff above town.
Fulton: The Kentucky Bend is an exclave surrounded by the Mississippi River and Tennessee — you can only drive there through another state.
Gallatin: Kentucky's smallest county by land area, yet it hosts the state's biggest racetrack, Kentucky Speedway.
Garrard: Temperance crusader Carry Nation, famous for smashing saloons with a hatchet, was born here in 1846.
Grant: Williamstown is home to the Ark Encounter, a full-scale ark replica that's one of the largest timber-frame structures anywhere.
Graves: Mayfield's Maplewood Cemetery holds the Wooldridge Monuments, a stone "procession that never moves" of a man, his family, and his horse.
Grayson: Nolin River Lake here feeds directly into the Mammoth Cave region's underground water system.
Green: Greensburg's 1804 courthouse is the oldest surviving courthouse west of the Allegheny Mountains.
Greenup: Author and poet laureate Jesse Stuart spent his life writing about W-Hollow, now a state nature preserve.
Hancock: Hawesville hosts one of the largest primary aluminum smelters in the United States.
Hardin: Fort Knox and the U.S. Bullion Depository sit here, guarding a large share of the nation's gold reserves.
Harlan: Black Mountain, at 4,145 feet, is the highest point in Kentucky.
Harrison: Robert Kirkman set "The Walking Dead" in his hometown of Cynthiana, which now hosts an annual zombie festival.
Hart: Munfordville was the birthplace of Simon Bolivar Buckner, a Confederate general who later became governor of Kentucky.
Henderson: John James Audubon ran a store here and studied the birds along the Ohio; a state park and museum honor him.
Henry: Writer and farmer Wendell Berry has worked the same hillside farm near Port Royal for more than half a century.
Hickman: Columbus-Belmont State Park preserves a mile-long iron chain the Confederacy stretched across the Mississippi to block Union boats.
Hopkins: Madisonville sat at the center of Western Kentucky's coalfield and still calls itself "The Best Town on Earth."
Jackson: A huge share of the county lies inside the Daniel Boone National Forest, making it one of Kentucky's most heavily wooded.
Jefferson: Louisville hosts the Kentucky Derby, the longest continuously held sporting event in the United States.
Jessamine: When High Bridge opened in 1877, it was the highest railroad bridge above a navigable stream in North America.
Johnson: Loretta Lynn grew up in Butcher Hollow near Van Lear; the cabin still stands and gives tours.
Kenton: John Roebling's Covington suspension bridge, finished in 1866, was his prototype for the Brooklyn Bridge.
Knott: Hindman Settlement School, founded in 1902, was the first rural settlement school in America.
Knox: Dr. Thomas Walker's 1750 cabin site near Barbourville marks the first structure built by Europeans in Kentucky.
Larue: Abraham Lincoln was born near Hodgenville in 1809, on a farm then part of Hardin County.
Laurel: London's World Chicken Festival fries chicken in a skillet more than ten feet across.
Lawrence: Fred M. Vinson of Louisa served as Chief Justice of the United States, plus Treasury Secretary and congressman.
Lee: Beattyville throws an annual Woolly Worm Festival, where the caterpillars are read as winter weather forecasts.
Leslie: Mary Breckinridge founded the Frontier Nursing Service in Hyden in 1925, sending nurse-midwives into the mountains on horseback.
Letcher: Whitesburg's Appalshop has been making films, records, and radio about Appalachian life since 1969.
Lewis: Vanceburg's Union soldier monument is one of very few Civil War Union memorials erected by a county in a former slave state.
Lincoln: One of Kentucky's three original counties, created in 1780, and site of the frontier outpost Fort Logan.
Livingston: Mantle Rock, a 30-foot sandstone arch, sheltered Cherokee travelers during the brutal winter of the Trail of Tears.
Logan: Jesse James pulled off one of his earliest daylight bank robberies in Russellville in 1868.
Lyon: The Kentucky State Penitentiary in Eddyville, opened in 1886, is known as the "Castle on the Cumberland."
Madison: Berea College, founded in 1855, was the first interracial and coeducational college in the South and still charges no tuition.
Magoffin: Named for Beriah Magoffin, the governor who tried to keep Kentucky neutral in the Civil War and resigned rather than pick a side.
Marion: Maker's Mark in Loretto was the first distillery ever designated a National Historic Landmark.
Marshall: Benton's Tater Day, running since 1843, is billed as the oldest continuous trade day festival in the United States.
Martin: President Lyndon Johnson announced the War on Poverty from a front porch in Inez in 1964.
Mason: Rosemary Clooney was born in Maysville, sang in local theaters as a girl, and is buried there.
McCracken: Paducah is a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art, anchored by the National Quilt Museum.
McCreary: The last county created in Kentucky (1912), and the only one with no incorporated cities at all.
McLean: The 1861 Battle of Sacramento was Nathan Bedford Forrest's first fight as a commanding officer.
Meade: John Hunt Morgan's raiders crossed the Ohio River at Brandenburg in 1863 on captured steamboats.
Menifee: Much of the Red River Gorge Geological Area, with its arches and cliffs, falls inside this county.
Mercer: Harrodsburg, founded in 1774, is the oldest permanent English settlement west of the Alleghenies.
Metcalfe: Named for Governor Thomas Metcalfe, a working stonemason nicknamed "Old Stone Hammer."
Monroe: Monroe County barbecue is its own regional style: hickory-smoked pork shoulder dipped in a fiery vinegar sauce.
Montgomery: Mount Sterling's Court Days trading fair dates to 1794 and still shuts down downtown every October.
Morgan: West Liberty's Sorghum Festival celebrates the cane syrup that was Appalachia's main sweetener for generations.
Muhlenberg: Birthplace of the Everly Brothers and Merle Travis, home of thumbpicking guitar, and the "Paradise" of John Prine's song.
Nelson: Bardstown calls itself the Bourbon Capital of the World and holds Federal Hill, the "My Old Kentucky Home" of the state song.
Nicholas: Named for George Nicholas, often called the father of Kentucky's first constitution.
Ohio: Bill Monroe, the father of bluegrass music, was born in the tiny community of Rosine.
Oldham: In La Grange, a freight train rumbles right down the middle of Main Street, several times a day.
Owen: Long nicknamed "Sweet Owen" by politicians who counted on its lopsided vote totals.
Owsley: One of Kentucky's least populous and most heavily forested counties, with woods covering the vast majority of its land.
Pendleton: Falmouth hosts the Kentucky Wool Festival, complete with sheep shearing contests and spinning demonstrations.
Perry: Both the county and its seat, Hazard, are named for the same man: Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry.
Pike: Kentucky's largest county by area, and the ground where the Hatfields and McCoys carried on their famous feud.
Powell: Natural Bridge State Resort Park's 65-foot sandstone arch has been a tourist draw since the 1890s.
Pulaski: Somerset calls itself the Houseboat Capital of the World, thanks to Lake Cumberland's 1,200 miles of shoreline.
Robertson: Kentucky's least populous county, with roughly 2,000 residents; Blue Licks Battlefield marks one of the last battles of the Revolution.
Rockcastle: Renfro Valley has broadcast live country music since 1939 and bills itself Kentucky's Country Music Capital.
Rowan: Morehead State runs a 21-meter radio telescope, one of the few university-owned deep space tracking antennas in the world.
Russell: Jamestown sits above Lake Cumberland, whose dam created one of the largest reservoirs east of the Mississippi.
Scott: Toyota's Georgetown plant is the company's largest vehicle manufacturing facility anywhere in the world.
Shelby: Shelbyville is the Saddlebred Capital of the World, with more American Saddlebreds bred nearby than anywhere else.
Simpson: Kentucky Downs in Franklin is one of the only all-turf racetracks in North America, with an unusual kidney-shaped course.
Spencer: Taylorsville Lake was one of the last major reservoirs built in Kentucky, finished in 1983.
Taylor: Campbellsville's former Fruit of the Loom plant became one of Amazon's earliest fulfillment centers in the country.
Todd: Jefferson Davis was born at Fairview, now marked by a 351-foot concrete obelisk you can ride an elevator to the top of.
Trigg: Cadiz throws a Country Ham Festival featuring what's claimed as the world's largest country ham biscuit.
Trimble: In 2012, engineers slid the entire 2,400-foot Milton-Madison bridge truss sideways onto new piers, a record-setting maneuver.
Union: German POWs held at Camp Breckinridge during WWII left behind murals that are now preserved as local art treasures.
Warren: In 2014 a sinkhole opened under the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green and swallowed eight cars.
Washington: The first county created after Kentucky became a state in 1792; Lincoln's parents were married here.
Wayne: Locals pronounce Monticello "Mont-i-SELL-o," not like Jefferson's house — a reliable way to spot an outsider.
Webster: Formed in 1860 from three neighboring counties and named for orator Daniel Webster; long a major coal producer.
Whitley: Cumberland Falls produces a moonbow on clear nights around the full moon — one of the only places on Earth where it happens predictably.
Wolfe: The Red River Gorge cliffs here draw sport climbers from around the world to some of the best sandstone routes anywhere.
Woodford: Versailles is pronounced "Ver-SALES," and Woodford Reserve sits on one of the oldest distilling sites in the country.
